title: Leaf litter: how much of it should become soil?
question: Which forest floor is right — the trees standing on their litter rather than sinking into it?
context_md:
You reported trees being buried by their own leaf fall. Reproduced here: `scene=forest`, one build, three frames each at **14,000 / 26,000 / 38,000**, same seed, cropped to the ground band.

The pipeline was 1:1 — a shed leaf becomes one litter cell, a settled litter cell weathers into one soil cell, and soil never weathers back. A plant builds its tissue from carbon fixed out of light, so that is matter entering the world from nothing and never leaving.

- **A** is current behaviour: every rotting leaf leaves a soil cell.
- **B** is the proposed 5%: one rotting leaf in twenty leaves soil, the rest leave nothing. That is roughly the real number — rotting is mostly the leaf being breathed away as CO2, and published humification puts the stabilised fraction in the low single digits to ~10%.

**What I am unsure of and want your eye on:** whether B now reads as *too* clean — a wood should still look like it has a floor, and I may have taken the litter layer with the soil.

**Please ignore** the root tangle and the canopy shape; neither changed, and the arms are the same seed.

One thing the numbers say that the picture does not: this only changes the *slope*. 5% of an unbounded stream is still unbounded, so a long enough run buries the trees either way. There is no sink for soil in the engine at all — a real fix needs one, and that is not this change.
